Abstract—Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems improve large language model (LLM) responses by retrieving relevant passages from external document stores and supplying them as generation context. When these documents contain personally identifiable information (PII), forwarding retrieved passages without protection exposes sensitive values to the generation model. This paper presents a privacy-aware RAG pipeline that inserts a lightweight detection-and-redaction guardrail between retrieval and generation. PDF documents are parsed and chunked, embedded using Sentence-Transformers, and indexed in ChromaDB. At query time, the top-k retrieved chunks are inspected using regular expression rules for structured identifiers and a spaCy-based Named Entity Recognition (NER) model for less structured contextual entities. Detected sensitive spans are replaced with entity-type placeholders before the sanitized context is passed to a Google Gemini model. A Streamlit interface exposes retrieval, detection, redaction, and answer-generation stages for inspection. On a labeled synthetic evaluation corpus of five PDF documents across 20 queries, the combined guardrail identified all 111 structured PII instances (True Positives = 111, False Negatives = 0, Recall = 100.00%) with 241 additional contextual entity predictions, resulting in a measured precision of 31.53% and an F1-score of 47.95%. The pipeline eliminated structured PII leakage across the 111 evaluated instances (a 100.00% empirical leakage reduction on predefined structured categories) while introducing an average pre-generation guardrail processing overhead of 2.51% (221.47 ms) over baseline retrieval. Because heuristic detection cannot guarantee complete protection against unmodeled entities, the approach is presented as an operational leakage-reduction guardrail rather than an absolute privacy guarantee. Quantitative multi-evaluator answer-quality assessment and end-to-end latency inclusive of generation time are identified as future work.
Keywords—Retrieval-Augmented Generation, privacy leakage, personally identifiable information, Named Entity Recognition, PII redaction, privacy guardrail, vector database, large language models.

Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate fluent responses but do not inherently have access to an organization's private or recently updated documents. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses this limitation by retrieving relevant passages from an external corpus and providing them to an LLM as context. RAG is therefore increasingly used for question answering over internal files, manuals, reports, and records. The same retrieval mechanism creates a privacy exposure point.

Organizational documents may contain names, email addresses, telephone numbers, identification numbers, financial information, addresses, and other sensitive content. When a retrieved passage is forwarded without inspection to a cloud-hosted or third-party LLM, the sensitive content becomes available at the generation boundary. Prior research has demonstrated that RAG systems can leak information from private retrieval databases, motivating protection mechanisms that address the retrieval-to-generation interface.

This work investigates a lightweight alternative to approaches that require differential-privacy budgets, entity perturbation, or changes to the underlying retrieval/generation models. The proposed guardrail combines deterministic regular-expression rules for structured identifiers with NER for named entities and redacts detected spans after retrieval but before generation. The design is model-agnostic with respect to the retriever and generator and can therefore be added to an existing RAG implementation.

The main contributions are: (1) a lightweight privacy-aware RAG architecture inserting a detection-and-redaction guardrail between retrieval and generation; (2) a hybrid regex-and-NER mechanism targeting both structured identifiers and contextual entities; (3) an interactive prototype exposing each pipeline stage for auditability; and (4) an empirical evaluation measuring detection performance, structured leakage reduction, pre-generation latency overhead, and a qualitative assessment of generative utility trade-offs.

work replaced the real private corpus with LLM-generated synthetic documents that preserve utility without real records. It removes the source of leakage entirely rather than filtering it later. The system considers a RAG deployment in which sensitive information may be present in documents uploaded by an organization and retrieved in response to user questions. The primary threat considered is unintended transmission of sensitive information from retrieved document context to the external LLM used for answer generation. The proposed guardrail establishes a privacy boundary between retrieval and generation. Retrieved chunks are inspected using
configured regex patterns and an NER model, and detected sensitive spans are replaced with entity-type placeholders before the context is forwarded to the LLM.

The protection is limited to sensitive information that can be detected by the configured rules and NER model. The original documents, stored chunks, and vector embeddings remain unchanged. Consequently, compromise of the source document store or vector database is outside the primary protection boundary. Similarly, sensitive information missed by the detectors may still reach the generator. The proposed system should therefore be interpreted as a leakage-reduction layer rather than a formal end-to-end privacy guarantee.

The proposed pipeline inserts one additional processing stage between the retriever and generator of a conventional RAG system: the privacy guardrail. Document ingestion, chunking, embedding, vector indexing, and semantic retrieval follow the standard RAG workflow. The guardrail receives the top-k retrieved chunks, detects configured sensitive entities, masks detected spans, and forwards only sanitized context to the generator.

The separation is intentional. Because the guardrail operates on retrieved text, the existing retriever and generator do not need to be retrained. The same mechanism can be enabled or disabled independently, allowing direct comparison between conventional RAG and privacy-aware RAG.

The first detector uses regular expressions for structured information whose surface form is relatively predictable. The prototype targets email addresses, telephone numbers, PAN numbers, Aadhaar numbers, bank-account-like values, IFSC-style codes, credit-card-like digit sequences, and configured government identification patterns. A matched value is replaced by a typed placeholder such as [EMAIL REDACTED] or [PHONE REDACTED].
The second detector uses a pre-trained

NER pipeline to identify less structured entities such as persons, organizations, and locations. Detected spans are replaced by entity-type placeholders. Regex detection is applied before NER so that structured values are handled explicitly and duplicate processing can be reduced.

The PII detection performance was evaluated using precision, recall, and F1-score across 20 evaluation queries spanning five domain-specific documents. The evaluation considered the structured PII values present in the retrieved contexts as the ground-truth benchmark. A detected span was classified as a True Positive (TP) when it exactly matched an annotated ground-truth PII instance.

Across the 20 queries, 111 structured PII instances were retrieved from the vector index. The proposed hybrid guardrail detected all 111 instances, resulting in 111 True Positives (TP = 111) and zero False Negatives (FN = 0), achieving a recall of 100.00%. Across the retrieved contexts, the detector produced 352 total predictions (TP + FP = 352), comprising 111 correct structured matches and 241 unmatched predictions (FP = 241). This yielded a measured precision of 31.53% and an F1-score of 47.95% (Table II).

Crucially, the 241 unmatched predictions cannot be automatically characterized as genuine detector errors. The ground-truth benchmark was constructed exclusively for structured PII categories (emails, telephone numbers, PAN, Aadhaar, account numbers, IFSC codes, credit card numbers, and government IDs). Meanwhile, the hybrid guardrail intentionally activates a spaCy NER model to identify less structured contextual entities, including person names, organizations, locations, and monetary amounts. When evaluated strictly against the structured PII benchmark, every valid contextual entity detected by the NER component (such as employee names, customer names, institution designations, and salary figures) is tallied as an unmatched prediction in the precision denominator, artificially depressing the precision metric. While genuine NER misclassifications do occur (e.g., tagging abbreviations such as 'PAN' as organization entities), a large proportion of these 241 detections represent valid contextual entities that were legitimately redacted per privacy policy, but were absent from the structured-only test key.

D. Qualitative Answer Comparison and Utility Analysis

To evaluate whether context redaction impedes downstream answer generation, identical question prompts were issued to both conventional RAG and privacy-aware RAG across all 20 test queries. In conventional RAG, the generator produces answers directly from raw retrieved passages, frequently exposing private identifiers verbatim in the generated response. In privacy-aware RAG, sensitive spans are replaced with entity-type placeholders prior to generation. Formal quantitative answer-quality scoring using independent human evaluators and inter-annotator agreement metrics is designated as immediate future work. In this study, we conduct a qualitative analysis of generated answer pairs to investigate the utility-privacy trade-off, as summarized in Table IV.

As illustrated in Table IV, the privacy guardrail successfully suppresses confidential identifiers (such as employee emails, phone numbers, PAN numbers, and synthetic bank accounts) while allowing the LLM to provide informative responses for procedural and descriptive queries. However, for questions explicitly querying named individuals (e.g., employee positions), redacting the subject's name to [PERSON REDACTED] breaks the relational link between query and context, causing the model to output a fallback response ('I couldn't find that information in the provided documents'). This qualitative finding demonstrates the fundamental operational trade-off between strict entity masking and query specificity.

Execution latency was evaluated to measure the computational overhead imposed by the privacy guardrail prior to generation. The latency measurements capture the pre-generation retrieval and guardrail pipeline, specifically dense semantic retrieval, regular-expression scanning, spaCy NER inference, and text redaction. The measurements intentionally exclude cloud API inference latency from Google Gemini. Latency overhead is defined as:

Across the 20 evaluation queries, baseline semantic retrieval averaged 8818.39 ms, while the combined retrieval-plus-guardrail pipeline averaged 9039.86 ms (Table V). The privacy guardrail introduced an average processing overhead of 221.47 ms, corresponding to a 2.51% increase over baseline retrieval. Because end-to-end cloud LLM generation typically incurs several seconds depending on network bandwidth and token length, the 221.47 ms guardrail latency constitutes an even smaller fraction of total user-perceived query time.

An error analysis was performed to identify the limitations of the proposed Regex- and NER-based privacy detection approach. Although the hybrid approach improves the detection of structured and contextual PII, certain false-positive and false-negative cases remain. These errors mainly arise from ambiguity in natural language, domain-specific terminology, and sensitive information that cannot be identified solely from surface patterns or conventional named-entity categories.

A representative false-positive case occurs when an ordinary word or contextual entity is incorrectly recognized as a sensitive entity by the NER model. For example, a person's name may be classified as a PERSON entity even when the occurrence is not privacy-sensitive in the given context. Similarly, a location may be detected as a geographic entity even when the location itself is not sensitive. Such cases can result in unnecessary redaction and reduce the

completeness of the retrieved context. False-negative cases may occur when sensitive information is expressed in an unusual format or when the information is not represented as a conventional named entity. For example, organization-specific employee identifiers, internal project codes, or domain-specific identifiers may not match predefined regular-expression patterns and may not be recognized by the NER model. Similarly, semantic information such as a person's medical condition, financial difficulty, or confidential professional information may be sensitive even though it does not correspond to a conventional PERSON, ORGANIZATION, or LOCATION entity.

These observations indicate that while regular expressions and NER provide effective detection for predictable and named entities, they do not provide exhaustive detection across all sensitive semantics. Representative error cases and practical mitigations are summarized in Table VI.

The experimental evaluation demonstrates that the proposed privacy-aware RAG framework reduces the exposure of sensitive information while preserving the core retrieval-augmented workflow. Across five synthetic domain documents and 20 evaluation queries, 111 structured PII instances were retrieved from the vector store.

The proposed Regex-and-NER detector correctly identified all 111 structured PII instances (True Positives = 111, False Negatives = 0), achieving a recall of 100.00%. The system generated 352 total predictions, of which 111 matched the structured ground truth, resulting in a measured precision of 31.53% and an F1-score of 47.95%. As detailed in Section VI-B, the measured precision reflects the evaluation of a hybrid detector against a structured-only ground-truth key. The 241 unmatched predictions largely represent valid contextual entities extracted by the NER module rather than defective detections. Standardizing multi-domain benchmarks that annotate both structured identifiers and contextual entities is essential for refining precision measurements in future work.

In the leakage reduction analysis, conventional RAG forwarded all 111 retrieved structured PII instances to the generator, whereas the proposed pipeline sanitized all 111 instances, achieving an empirical leakage reduction of 100.00% across the test corpus. This measurement is strictly restricted to the 111 predefined structured PII instances within the synthetic benchmark. Heuristic pattern matching and statistical NER cannot guarantee complete privacy protection across novel document formats or unstructured disclosures, highlighting the need to treat the pipeline as an operational leakage-reduction layer rather than a formal guarantee.

The qualitative answer-quality evaluation confirmed that procedural and informational inquiries retain high utility following PII masking, but queries focused on redacted entity names suffer utility loss. Because human evaluator ratings must not be unsubstantiated, quantitative scoring on multi-point rubrics is designated as future work with formal inter-annotator agreement.

The latency evaluation demonstrated that baseline retrieval required an average of 8818.39 ms, while the retrieval-plus-guardrail pipeline required 9039.86 ms, representing a modest pre-generation overhead of 2.51% (221.47 ms). These measurements reflect local pre-generation processing and intentionally exclude cloud LLM generation time, which further reduces the proportional overhead in practice.

In summary, the hybrid architecture provides an effective, lightweight privacy guardrail that can be integrated into existing RAG deployments without model retraining. Future work includes expanding evaluation to larger heterogenous corpora, implementing context-preserving surrogate replacement, and conducting rigorous multi-annotator answer-quality evaluations.
